en: Dinakari:

[The objection that] there would be a loss of the status of being an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*) [is answered as follows]. Regarding the phrase "with respect to which effect": [it means] with respect to that which is delimited by a particular property (*dharmāvacchinna*).
The meaning of "dependent" (*pratītya*) is as follows: "by which form" means "by the delimitation of which form.

And thus, [the definition applies] when there is the state of being the deliminator of the qualificandum-ness (*viśeṣyatāvacchedakatva*) in the apprehension of the necessary antecedent existence (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) as determined by that property (*dharmāvacchinna*).

The meaning of "first" is that, while existing, it lacks independent positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with respect to that which is delimited by a particular property; this constitutes being "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) with respect to that which is delimited by that property.
The term "existing" (sati) is included to exclude the second type of otherwise-established cause, such as the color and form of a staff. [Example: the conjunction of the potsherds...

In order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the potsherd (*kapāla*), which also possesses such a delimitor of the qualificandum (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) when one grasps [the cognition] "that which precedes the jar" and so forth, the term "qualificandum" (*viśeṣya*) is used;

however, it must be "the cause. And here, causality (*kāraṇatva*) consists in possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) independently; by that [definition],... [Dinakarī, page 92].

It is not self-dependent (*nātmāśraya*). [This is because] while it lacks positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to its own effect as an independent factor, it possesses the status of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) in the apprehension of its own necessary antecedence (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*)— as delimited by that cause— with respect to its own effect.

The meaning is that this effect is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) with respect to that [cause]. This refers to the qualificand-ness residing in the conjunction of the potsherds (*kapāla-saṃyoga*), which belongs to the apprehension of its being a prior-occupant (*pūrvavṛtti*)— as in the case of the statement "the conjunction of the potsherds is a prior-occupant of the jar."

The "existence" (sat) portion [of the definition] is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the conjunction with a skull (*kapāla-saṃyoga*), because that is delimited by the skull itself.
The "particularized" (*viśeṣya*) portion is included to exclude [properties such as] "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*).

In this context, if it were stated that [the cause] possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) necessitated by the positive and negative concomitance of the other [factors], [then the definition would be too narrow].

It should be understood that although the first and second types of *anyathāsiddhi* (redundant causality) are included [in the definition], they are presented separately for the sake of clarifying the student's intellect. "In relation to another" (*anyaṃ prati*) means in relation to another thing that is not conducive to the result (*phalānanuguṇa*). Therefore, it is not...
There is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to the potter's father, because the fourth type of "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) is not exhausted [in his case].

He raises an objection: "By being the substratum of sound. The sense is that there is no absence of the third type of "otherwise-established" (defined as) "being established in relation to another. [The author replies: "The fifth [type of otherwise-established]. *Dinakarī*. *Pañcamī* (the fifth).

The meaning is that [the inference] is based on such [premises] as "that which is necessarily established as an invariably preceding factor," and so forth. Although [sound] is indeed [established] by means of an auxiliary favorable condition consisting of the apprehension of the causal relation— namely, the inference "sound is produced by a substance, because it is a produced quality"— [the following applies].

Having apprehended that sound has space as its substratum through the inference "sound is dependent on a substance because it is a quality," one must then apprehend that [space] exists prior to the jar in that capacity; and thus,
it is only by apprehending that space exists prior to sound that [the pervasion is established].

Although only the third type of *anyathāsiddhi* (redundant causality) is possible due to the apprehension of the pot's existence prior [to its effect], nevertheless, if the phrase "with respect to another" (*anyaṃ prati*) were taken in its literal sense, there would be *anyathāsiddhi* of the sacrifice with respect to the *apūrva* (the unseen merit);

for one could only grasp the causal efficacy of the sacrifice toward heaven by first grasping its priority [in time] with respect to that [heaven], and then, through the impossibility otherwise of what has been grasped as a cause.

It is necessary to intend the following extent [of the definition]: because the apūrva is postulated as the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the sacrifice, for whatever has the status of being a producer of something with respect to another by way of a form consisting of its prior existence, that thing is "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*) with respect to that other thing by way of that form. This applies to the sacrifice.

Even though the apūrva (unseen potency) is otherwise established as a cause by way of its being the generator of heaven— which is defined by its existence prior to heaven— there is no lack of being otherwise established in its being a cause by way of its nature as a sacrifice (*yāga*). And likewise, even though the ether (*gagana*) is otherwise established as a cause by way of its being the generator of sound— which is defined by its existence prior to sound— ...

The intention is that if [the ether] were taken as a cause by virtue of being the substratum of sound not produced by conjunction, then a third type of "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) would be impossible. Even if the ether were a cause with respect to a jar by way of its being the substratum of sound, or by its being a substance distinct from the eight substances, etc., it would still be a case of the third type of "otherwise-established," namely, being otherwise-established with respect to something else.

Some maintain that because the status of being a prior condition (*pūrvavṛttitva*) is not established for that which is grasped as a prior condition relative to something else, there is no "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the sacrifice with respect to the *apūrva*.
Regarding the phrase "such as the quality of being *ka*," due to the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanābhāva*), [the cause would apply] to many phonemes.

Because [the property of] being the delimiting condition of causality would involve complexity (*gaurava*) and because phonemes are not present at all times, he says: "Or it is the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "with respect to that which produces an effect": here too, if one were to state "with respect to another," and so forth...

Although the third and fourth types of "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) are included within [the first two], there is no purpose in designating them separately by adding the qualifiers of "not being conducive to the effect" and "being conducive to it," even so, [this distinction is made] as in the *Dinakarī*.
It was stated thus for the sake of clarifying the student's intellect. Regarding the phrase "necessarily postulated" (*avaśyaklṛpta*):

since the production of odor can be accounted for by the prior absence of odor (*gandhaprāgabhāva*)—which is necessarily postulated as the determinant (*avacchedaka*) of the universal "odor-ness" (*gandhatva*)—the prior absences of color and other qualities coexisting with it are *anyathāsiddha* (redundant) with respect to the odors produced by baking (*pākaja-gandha*). Thus...

The meaning is that, since the production of a jar is possible through the staff and other such factors—which are necessarily established as its invariable antecedents—a donkey is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) with respect to that production.
[Objection: But surely, by the prior absence of color produced by baking (pākajarūpa-prāgabhāva), which is necessarily established as an invariable antecedent...

If it is argued that, in the case of the production of a fragrance from a flower, the prior non-existence of fragrance would be "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddhi) by the prior non-existence of color,

and that if one were to state that its causality is necessarily postulated, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), they reply: here, "necessarily postulated" means having the nature of being a light and necessary antecedent.
The object of cognition (*bodhya*) is lightness (*laghutva*), which is established through presence (*upasthiti*) and through relation (*saṃbandha*).

Among these, the first [type of lightness] exists in relation to magnitude (*mahattva*) because it inheres in multiple substances; the second exists in the prior absence of odor (*gandha-prāgabhāva*) in relation to the prior absence of color (*rūpa-prāgabhāva*) with respect to odor. This is because, as stated in the *Dinakarī*, there is the existence of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) consisting of odor.

[The reason for this is] its rapid proximity [to the effect]. Thirdly, it is "the stick" (daṇḍa) in relation to the form and other qualities of the stick. This is because gravity belongs to a causal chain composed of the conjunction of the stick with its own substratum and so forth.
Now, one might object: since it is seen that [this definition] is established elsewhere in other treatises, why is it said here that it is "necessarily established"?
He states the result of that established view with the words "for this very reason.

The sense is that otherwise, since magnitude (*mahattva*) lacks a fixed antecedence established elsewhere than in its being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*), its being "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of magnitude would not occur. Here, "being composed of multiple substances" refers to...

It is not "inherence in multiple substances," for since that exists even in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), it would follow that the dyad is perceptible. Nor is it "inherence in that which inheres [in multiple substances]," because that is absent in the self (*ātman*), and thus the perception of the self would be untenable. Rather, it is "the state of being a substance distinct from atoms."
This is the point to be understood. By that [definition], the fifth type of "otherwise-established" (anyathāsiddha) is excluded.
For others—the staff, the non-staff, space, the potter, and the father—their purpose is already served [by other means].
This is the summary. The term "niyata" (invariable), and so forth, is used to exclude irregular things such as a donkey.

Nor should it be argued that the term "restricted" (*niyata*) is redundant because the non-restricted donkey and so forth are excluded by the fifth type of "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) alone; for since there is no single [criterion] such as "being necessarily postulated," the exclusion consists in the difference from whatever things authoritative persons do not conventionally treat as causes.

The intention is that since donkeys and the like are excluded by the very term "fixed" (*niyata*) through its necessity of being applied [to the cause], the distinction of that [non-fixed] entity does not enter [into the definition]. Furthermore, "antecedence" (*pūrvavartitva*) means immediate antecedence; by this, antecedence mediated by an interval is excluded.

For this very reason, the authors of the treatises justify the existence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) by establishing that, since it is impossible for sacrifice and the like to be the direct cause of heaven, the sacrifice must be related to the *apūrva* in order to fulfill the requirement of being an immediate antecedent. Otherwise, since the sacrifice itself would possess a necessary antecedence without contradiction, there would be no grounds for postulating an *apūrva*. Nor is such a [position]...

It must be explained how the apprehension of a positive deviation (anvaya-vyabhicāra) is an obstacle to the apprehension of causality, given that while the apprehension of a negative deviation (vyatireka-vyabhicāra) is indeed an obstacle to the grasping of the element of necessity because it involves the awareness of the absence of the object to be grasped, such is not the case for the apprehension of a positive deviation.

Because [the definition] beginning with "avaśyaklṛpta" (necessarily postulated) serves as the basis for the knowledge of "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*): when all other causes of that effect are present, the absence of that effect occurs through the absence of that which is necessarily postulated as its invariable antecedent; thus, there is the knowledge of its being otherwise-established by means of that which is necessarily postulated. However, the Navya-Naiyāyikas [state]:

If being a cause consisted in possessing a property that delimits an invariably antecedent state that is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*), it would follow that the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is a cause by virtue of its specific individuality (*tattadvyaktitvena*). Furthermore, the possession of a collection of differences from those specific individuals where the conventional usage of "causality" does not apply can only be known by an omniscient being.

It should be known that [the opponent's view] is also not tenable, namely: "That [causality] is the possession of a property (dharma) qualified by the effect through the relation of being a collection (*kūṭa*) of the various distinct individual instances (*vyakti*). This is because there is doubt regarding whether that [collection] constitutes a relation.
Therefore, they say that causality (*kāraṇatva*) is indeed a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). That is incorrect; for if causality were something additional...

[Answer: No, because [if that were so], there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the perception of a staff and the like at all times. Nor should it be argued that a property such as "being not otherwise established" (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of that [universality].
Since such knowledge of the property (dharma) is necessary, it is appropriate that it alone takes the form of the apprehension of causality;

or rather, let the state of being a cause (kāraṇatva) be simply the nature of the staff and so forth, because when that [nature] is apprehended as related to the effect such as a jar, the aforementioned property serves as its manifestor (vyañjaka). Others, however, [hold...]
They [the Naiyāyikas] stated that [causality] consists in possessing positive and negative concomitance at times prior to the time of the effect’s positive and negative concomitance.

That is incorrect; because it lacks pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which are not the causes of pleasure and the like, since a negative concomitance in the form of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is impossible there. 19 || 20 || 21 || 22 || Dinakarī: [In the] root-text...
It was stated that [the definition] consists in being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) whose function resides solely in qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*);

however, that is incorrect because it does not apply (*avyāpti*) to the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, he explains the root text with the intent of showing its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—namely, "being a non-inherent cause. He says "or rather" (*athavā*) because he considers it improper to state a dissimilarity within a section dealing with similarities (*sādharmya*).

The term "subsisting" (*vṛtti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to a substance that possesses the genus (*jāti*) characterized by being a distinct substance (*satabhinnadravyatva*). To exclude over-extension to that very same [substance] by taking the genus of existence (*sattājāti*), the phrase "distinct from existence" (*satābhinnā*) is used. To exclude over-extension to that very same [substance] by taking the property (*dharma*) characterized by being either a substance or a quality (*dravyaguṇānyataratva*), the word "genus" (*jāti*) is used.

The intended meaning of "subsisting" (*vṛttitva*) and "possessing a universal" (*jātimatva*) is by way of inherence (*samavāya*). Therefore, because substanceness (*dravyatva*) subsists in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth by way of temporal relation (*kālika*), and because substance (*dravya*) possesses qualityness (*guṇatva*) and so forth by way of temporal relation, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substance. [Objection: But what about the sky (*gagana*) and so forth?

Because of the worldly usage [of expressions] such as "it exists at all times," the Dinakarī [states that] since even eternal substances possess the property of being dependent (āśritatva) by means of the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*), the root text’s statement "other than eternal substances" is incorrect; therefore, it says: "The property of being dependent [is defined] by means of relations such as inherence (*samavāya*)."
"By a relation other than the temporal relation that restricts being the substratum of all" means "by way of being a qualifier.

This means "by way of temporal qualification. Here, the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) is the state of being distinct from eternal substances. Nor [is there over-extension], because even an atom exists [in space] by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

There is over-extension (ativyāpti) to the atom, because its conjunction is a determinant of occurrence (vṛttiniyāmaka). He clarifies the meaning indicated by the word "tu" (but/however) in the root text—"of the nine, beginning with earth"—with the words "now" (idānīm).
Dinakarī: Now, [it may be argued that] since the meaning of a verbal root is an action (*kriyā*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in that case. Therefore—

He says: "Possession of action" means possession of velocity (*vega*). This [possession of velocity] is the cause of priority and posteriority produced by direction (*dik*), based on the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that "this is proximate to that.
It is the cause of priority and posteriority produced by time (*kāla*), based on [the cognition] that "this is connected with fewer moments of time than that."

Having raised the objection that there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because distance (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) do not arise where relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) has not arisen, he refutes this with the words "And not... and so forth. This is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the self (*ātman*).

[The definition] ends with the term *samānādhikaraṇa*. In that very context, the phrase "pervaded by substancehood" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is included to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking [the property of] existence (*sattā*) as the [qualifier]. Furthermore, the genus (*jāti*) must also be qualified by being other than substancehood; thus, there is no over-extension by taking substancehood—which is pervaded by substancehood—as the [qualifier]. [The word] "inferior" (*apakṛṣṭa*)...
The meaning is: "possessing a magnitude that is not all-pervasive. By this, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of an atom (paramāṇu).

Some also maintain that "corporeality" (mūrtatva)—which is the genus (jāti) that delimits the capacity to produce action—is [the definition]. "And that" means: "and that aforementioned corporeality. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tu" (but/whereas). "As before" means as previously stated.
"Like that which possesses the intended meaning stated in the passage beginning with 'co-inherent with priority and posteriority' (paratvāparatvasamānādhikaraṇa...
means: like that which possesses the intended meaning stated in the passage beginning with "co-inherent with priority and posteriority. ||25||

Anticipating the objection that [the definition] is impossible because there is no motion in time and so forth, he says: "sarvamūrta" (all corporeal). This refers to the property of being the ultimate magnitude (paramamahattva), which is the object of the cognition "I am great," and which is common to both the ether and the atom. (Dinakari)

Following the opinion of the author of the *Ṭīkā* that even if the nature of being a genus (*jātitva*) were possible, the size of the self (*ātmaparimāṇa*) is unfit [to be a genus], he says: "limitation" (*apakarṣa*).
Although, among the atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is only the dimension of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) that is the locus of limitation, and not the dimension of the atom itself.

Even so, it should be understood that the definition refers to "the state of having a magnitude greater than the smallest" (mahat-parimāṇatva), which excludes over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the atom (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of an external sense-organ" (*bahirindriya*): the word "external" (*bahiḥ*) is included to prevent over-extension to the self (*ātman*).

Furthermore, it is included to prevent over-extension to time (*kāla*) and other such entities, which possess conjunctions (*saṃyoga*) and the like belonging to a class perceivable by external sense-organs.
Regarding the term "viśeṣa" (specific): the nature of being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) will be explained in the section defining qualities.

The word "quality" (*guṇa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) that would otherwise apply to substantiality (*dravyatva*). He states the purpose of including "empirical" (*laukika*) as follows: "by this... In the cognition "the pot is known," with respect to the aspect of the knowledge that serves as the qualifier (*prakārībhūta-jñāna*), [the definition applies].
The meaning is that there is no worldly objectivity (*laukikī viṣayatā*) for the eye and other [senses] therein, because of the absence of worldly sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*). (Dinakari)
He states the result of introducing the suitability of essential nature (*svarūpayogyatā*) with the words "or not" (*na vā*).
Now, if the color and other qualities of an atom are indeed suitable, why is there no perception of them? To this he replies: "in [the presence of] largeness" (*mahattve*).

This means that for the perception of a substance-inherent [quality], [largeness] is required by way of the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), given its status as an ordinary object of perception.

The meaning is that because the magnitude of the cause is absent in things such as atoms, those are not objects of ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*). Now, one might raise the objection that there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding the eyes and other [senses], since the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as color residing in the sense organs are unmanifest (*anudbhūta*) and thus unfit to be grasped by external senses. Anticipating this:

Due to simplicity, [the author] says: "Or rather" (*athavā*). And in this alternative, the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the mind (*manas*), which would otherwise occur by taking spatial priority and posteriority (*daiśika-paratvāparatva*) into account. "Possession of touch" (*sparśavattva*) is [to be understood] by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

[The definition of matter is] "possessing touch" (sparśavattva). [Regarding the phrase] "inherently causal substance" (dravyasamavāyikāraṇa) and so forth: the term "pervaded by substanceness" (dravyatvavyāpya) is included in order to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to space (gagana), which possesses existence (sattā) and so on. Regarding the word "embodied beings" (śarīrin) in the root text "of space and embodied beings," he says "of space and selves" (ākāśātmanām), with the intention that the word "embodied being" refers to the self (ātman).

In order to apply the definition to the object of definition, he establishes the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of word-cognition and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "of space" (*ākāśasya*). He states "and momentariness" because he does not accept that a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) can be momentary. [He adds this] for the purpose of excluding [the case of] jars and the like.

"Existing at the third moment" (tṛtīyakṣaṇavṛtti). "Existing after itself" (svottaravṛtti): the word "self" (sva) refers to that which is intended to be destroyed; "existing after it" means existing at the second moment of that [destruction]; the meaning is: because of being destructible by that specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) which exists at its second moment. And here, where [the relation] is the relation of counter-positive-ness (pratiyogitā-sambandha)...

The destruction of a particular quality (viśeṣaguṇa) in a capable pervasive substance (yogyavibhu) occurs through the relation of co-location (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and the relation of being immediately antecedent; thus,
a particular quality acts as the destroyer by way of co-location.

The object of attainment (*bodhya*). By including "fitness" (*yogyatva*) as a delimiting factor of the state of being an effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the destruction of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by penances and the like. And fitness consists in being either the object of a worldly direct perception (*laukikasākṣātkāra*) or a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).

Alternatively, it is the state of being devoid of a genus that transcends the senses. [In the *Dinakarī*: The term "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*) is used to exclude deviation in the case of the destruction of color and so forth;
the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is used to exclude deviation in the case of the destruction of conjunction and so forth.
Because "fitness" (*yogyatva*) and "specificity" (*viśeṣatva*) are included in the delimiting factor of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), there is no [fault].

Due to the inclusion of the relation of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) in the third moment— caused by the conjunction of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) arising in the second moment— there is no destruction of heterogeneous [qualities] such as sound, or cognitions, desires, and so forth. Furthermore, this is because of the inclusion of the relation of "occurring immediately prior to itself" (*svāvyavahitapūrvavṛttitva*).

There is no destruction of knowledge and the other qualities by a desire and so forth existing at the time of their production. Some, however, say that because ownership (svatva) terminates in each specific individual, each respective quality is the destroyer of that respective quality; they further claim that for the cognition of relative number (apekṣābuddhi), the perception of duality is the cause of its destruction. Others, however, [say...]

The state of being destroyed is defined by the quality of being a specific quality of a pervasive substance (vibhu-viśeṣa-guṇa) produced at this very moment; the state of being the destroyer is defined by the quality of being a specific quality of a pervasive substance existing in the moment immediately following this moment.

However, in the case of the destruction of a relative cognition (apekṣā-buddhi), there is a specific causal complex consisting of the perception of duality; therefore, [the destruction occurs] in the moment following the relative cognition.

Even when the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) is present, there is no deficiency; for the final cognition and so forth are themselves the destroyers, qualified by their existence in the subsequent moment. Furthermore, they say that this [principle] is common to all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) produced in this very moment.

Having established the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of sound, he establishes these same properties for cognition and other mental states as well— beginning with the word "thus" (*evam*). He explains the meaning with the words "and thus" (*itthaṃca*), intending two definitions [of momentariness] in order to avoid the redundancy of the term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).

Regarding the statement "it was said [to be] non-pervasive" (*avyāpyavṛtti*): one should not object that since qualities such as color (*rūpa*) are also temporally non-pervasive, how can they be excluded? For by the term "non-pervasive," spatial non-pervasiveness is intended. Regarding the statement "it was said [to be] a specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

And the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇas*) are those to be mentioned later as: "The group of six beginning with cognition (*buddhi*) and ending with touch, viscidity, natural fluidity, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound—these are the specific qualities. Their definition, however, will be stated in the section on the determination of qualities (*guṇa-nirūpaṇa*). As for that which... [text fragment]... Dinakarī. (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

The definition "possessing a specific quality that does not have pervasive occurrence" is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to God (*īśvara*), because His qualities do possess pervasive occurrence. That is not so; for by the term "non-pervasively occurring," what is meant is the state of possessing a genus (*jāti*) that is subsumed under the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and which resides in that which has non-pervasive occurrence.
Because it is intended [to exclude atoms]. Regarding the phrase "subsisting in four moments":

those produced things such as jars that subsist for four moments—whatever universal (jāti) such as "knowability" (*jñānatva*) does not subsist in them, a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as cognition (*jñāna*) possesses that universal; since the possession of that [specific quality] exists in the self (*ātman*) and so forth, the definition is fully applicable.

And here, "subsistence" (vṛttitva) is intended in the sense of inherence (samavāya). Therefore, there is no defect even though the property of being a cognition (jñānatva) subsists in all produced things by way of temporal relation (kālika-sambandha).

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "subsistence" (vṛti) is for the purpose of avoiding the impossibility [of the definition] since the property of being a cognition and so forth subsist in produced things [by temporal relation]. This is the meaning of that [phrase].

The meaning is: "because it is a category possessing momentary specific qualities. Now, one might object: having disregarded existence for three moments, there is no purpose in pursuing existence up to four moments; nor is there a difference of parsimony (lāghava) or complexity (gaurava) between the numbers three and four.
If one were to adopt the number four, it must be stated that "desire" (icchā) is the restrictive factor.
However, since the parsimony consisting in being the first to be presented is possible in the case of the number three, he says:
"the enumerative cognition" (apekṣābuddhi). Thus, when the property of existing for three moments is introduced, [the property of] being a cognition (jñānatva)...

The meaning is that there would be no inclusion [of the definition]. He states the purpose of the phrase "not residing in what is produced in four moments" as follows: "But color-ness (rūpatva) and so forth. "Its exclusion" means the exclusion of the universal (jāti) color-ness. And thus, [the definition applies] to that which possesses a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) characterized by the universal color-ness.
The meaning is that the over-extension (ativyāpti) [of the definition] to jars and the like has been refuted. He states the purpose of the term "produced" (janyā): "by the Lord," etc.
